title: Back Pain Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing back pain, recognising serious pathology, performing focused examination and interpreting common examination patterns.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, local pathways or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: New bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
New saddle or perineal sensory disturbance.
Bilateral or progressive lower-limb neurological symptoms.
Objective motor weakness, foot drop or unsafe gait.
Fever, systemic illness or risk factors for spinal infection.
Significant trauma, focal bony tenderness or fragility-fracture risk.
Known cancer or features suggesting spinal metastases or metastatic spinal cord compression.
Abdominal, vascular, renal or hip pathology presenting as back pain.
items.importantLimitation: A reassuring single symptom, examination finding or test does not independently exclude serious spinal pathology.

sections.title: History prompts
sections.intro: Use focused questions to characterise the pain and identify serious pathology or an alternative source.

items.title: Pain characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Exact location and whether pain is central, paraspinal, flank, abdominal, buttock or groin.
Onset: sudden or gradual; traumatic, lifting or spontaneous.
Duration, progression and whether constant or intermittent.
Radiation into one or both legs and whether symptoms extend below the knee.
Aggravating and relieving factors, including movement, position, coughing or straining.
Pain at rest, night pain and sleep disturbance.
Effect on standing, walking, transfers, work and self-care.

items.title: Neurological and cauda equina symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: New difficulty initiating urination, reduced bladder sensation, retention or overflow leakage.
New bowel dysfunction or reduced awareness of defecation.
New saddle, perineal or genital sensory change.
New sexual dysfunction associated with the episode.
Bilateral sciatica, bilateral sensory symptoms or progressive weakness.
Foot drop, falls, gait change or loss of hand function suggesting more extensive neurological disease.

items.title: Serious pathology and alternative-source screen
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors, recent significant infection, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use or recent spinal procedure.
Known cancer, unexplained weight loss or progressive non-mechanical pain.
Significant trauma, osteoporosis, fragility fracture or prolonged corticosteroid use.
Abdominal pain, collapse, syncope, pulsatile symptoms or vascular risk.
Flank pain, haematuria, urinary symptoms, vomiting or anuria.
Hip or groin pain, inability to weight-bear or recent fall.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive or evolving features should change disposition and trigger the appropriate emergency or urgent pathway.

items.title: Cauda equina syndrome
urgentFeatures: New bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
Progressive or bilateral lower-limb neurological deficit.
implications: Immediate referral for emergency assessment and MRI pathway.
items.importantLimitation: No single normal symptom, examination finding, rectal examination or bladder scan safely excludes cauda equina syndrome.

items.title: Spinal infection
urgentFeatures: Fever or systemic illness with new back pain.
Recent bacteraemia, spinal procedure or surgery.
Constant progressive pain, focal tenderness or new neurological deficit.
implications: Possible discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis or spinal epidural abscess; urgent hospital assessment is required.

items.title: Vertebral fracture
urgentFeatures: Significant trauma or acute focal pain after minor trauma in a person at fragility-fracture risk.
Focal midline bony tenderness, deformity or neurological deficit.

items.title: Malignancy and metastatic spinal cord compression
urgentFeatures: Known cancer with new severe, progressive or night pain.
Gait disturbance, weakness, sensory loss or bladder or bowel dysfunction.

items.title: Abdominal or vascular emergency
urgentFeatures: Sudden severe back or abdominal pain, collapse, hypotension, pallor or diaphoresis.
Pulsatile abdominal mass, pulse deficit or a cold pale painful limb.
implications: Immediate emergency escalation; do not pursue routine spinal imaging.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Compare both sides. Interpret findings alongside the history, observations, risk factors, progression and functional ability.

items.title: General assessment and mobility
howToTest: Assess overall appearance, distress and systemic illness.
Record observations where clinically indicated, including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation.
Observe the patient sitting, standing, transferring and walking.
Assess whether pain is reproducible with movement or position.
Reassess mobility after analgesia where appropriate.
normal: Haemodynamically stable and not systemically unwell.
Able to transfer and mobilise safely.
Pain is mechanically reproducible without objective neurological deficit.
abnormal: Fever, hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis or systemic deterioration.
Collapse, inability to stand, unsafe gait or rapidly worsening function.
Pain that is constant, disproportionate or unrelated to movement.
implications: Systemic illness may indicate infection or another non-musculoskeletal cause.
Collapse or haemodynamic compromise may indicate vascular or intra-abdominal pathology.
Inability to mobilise safely changes disposition even when no specific diagnosis is confirmed.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Systemic illness.
Haemodynamic compromise.
Unsafe mobility.
Non-spinal referred pathology.

items.title: Inspection and palpation
howToTest: Inspect posture, spinal alignment, bruising, swelling, wounds, deformity, scars, rash and muscle spasm.
Palpate the midline vertebrae and paraspinal muscles.
Assess for focal warmth, swelling and renal-angle tenderness where relevant.
normal: No deformity, bruising, swelling, rash or focal midline tenderness.
Possible mild paraspinal tenderness or spasm without bony tenderness.
implications: Focal bony tenderness after trauma or in a patient with fragility-fracture risk may indicate vertebral fracture.
Warmth, swelling or focal tenderness with systemic features may indicate infection.
Renal-angle tenderness may indicate renal or urinary pathology.
A vesicular rash may indicate herpes zoster.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Vertebral fracture.
Spinal infection.
Renal or urinary source.
Herpes zoster.

items.title: Gait and functional testing
howToTest: Observe normal walking.
Ask the patient to stand from a chair without using their arms where safe.
Ask the patient to walk on their heels, then on their toes.
Look for foot drop, foot slap, knee buckling, leg dragging, asymmetry or a broad-based or stiff gait.
normal: Symmetrical gait.
Able to stand, heel-walk and toe-walk bilaterally.
No objective functional weakness.
abnormal: Knee buckling due to true weakness.
New broad-based, spastic or markedly unsteady gait.
implications: Difficulty heel-walking may indicate ankle dorsiflexion weakness, commonly involving L4 or L5.
Difficulty toe-walking may indicate plantarflexion weakness, commonly involving S1.
A spastic or broad-based gait may indicate spinal cord or central neurological pathology.

items.title: Lower-limb power
items.summary: Test against resistance and compare both sides. Consider pain inhibition and repeat testing if effort is limited.
howToTest: Hip flexion: ask the patient to lift the thigh while you apply downward resistance over the distal thigh.
Knee extension: ask the patient to straighten the knee while you apply resistance at the lower leg.
Ankle dorsiflexion: ask the patient to pull the foot towards the shin while you push down over the dorsum of the foot.
Great-toe extension: stabilise the foot, ask the patient to lift the great toe, then apply downward resistance.
Ankle plantarflexion: ask the patient to push the foot down against resistance; use repeated heel raises where safe.
normal: Power is 5/5 and symmetrical.
The patient can sustain movement against appropriate resistance.
Functional movements agree with isolated power testing.
abnormal: Power below 5/5 that is not explained by pain alone.
Foot drop, weak great-toe extension or inability to perform a heel raise.
Weakness affecting more than one nerve-root pattern.
implications: Weak knee extension may indicate L3 or L4 radiculopathy or femoral nerve dysfunction.
Weak ankle dorsiflexion or great-toe extension may indicate L4 or L5 involvement.
Weak plantarflexion may indicate S1 involvement.
Bilateral, progressive or multi-root weakness raises concern for cauda equina or spinal cord pathology.
items.importantLimitation: Pain may inhibit effort. Do not label weakness as pain-limited until objective neurological weakness has been actively reconsidered.

items.title: Lower-limb sensation
howToTest: Use light touch and compare matching points on both legs.
Test the anterior thigh, medial knee and lower leg, dorsum of the foot and great toe, lateral foot and posterior calf.
Ask whether sensation is equal, reduced, absent or unusually painful.
Look for a consistent pattern rather than relying on one isolated point.
normal: Sensation is symmetrical and intact.
No consistent dermatomal deficit.
abnormal: Reduced sensation over the medial lower leg, dorsum of the foot, great toe or lateral foot.
A sensory level or pattern that does not fit a single lumbar nerve root.
implications: Medial lower-leg sensory loss may support L4 involvement.
Dorsum-of-foot or great-toe sensory loss may support L5 involvement.
Lateral-foot sensory loss may support S1 involvement.
Bilateral, widespread or non-dermatomal objective loss may indicate more extensive neurological pathology.

items.title: Lower-limb reflexes
howToTest: Knee reflex: keep the leg relaxed and strike the patellar tendon below the kneecap.
Ankle reflex: slightly dorsiflex the foot and strike the Achilles tendon.
Compare both sides and interpret alongside power, sensation and gait.
normal: Knee and ankle reflexes are present and broadly symmetrical.
abnormal: A clearly reduced or absent reflex on one side.
implications: A reduced knee reflex may support L3 or L4 radiculopathy.
A reduced ankle reflex may support S1 radiculopathy.
Brisk reflexes or sustained clonus may indicate upper motor-neurone or spinal cord pathology.
items.importantLimitation: Reflexes may be reduced by age, peripheral neuropathy or previous disease. An isolated absent reflex is less important than a new asymmetrical pattern.

items.title: Straight-leg raise
howToTest: Position the patient supine.
Keep the knee straight and slowly raise the leg by flexing the hip.
Ask where symptoms are felt and whether the patient's familiar leg pain is reproduced.
Compare both sides.
For crossed straight-leg raise, lift the unaffected leg and assess whether this reproduces pain in the symptomatic leg.
normal: Hamstring tightness or mild back discomfort only.
No reproduction of familiar radicular pain.
abnormal: The patient's familiar shooting or electric leg pain is reproduced, usually below the knee.
Symptoms are reproduced approximately between 30 and 70 degrees.
Crossed straight-leg raise reproduces pain in the opposite symptomatic leg.
implications: A positive test supports lumbosacral nerve-root irritation.
A positive crossed test is more specific for significant nerve-root irritation or disc prolapse.
items.importantLimitation: A normal straight-leg raise does not exclude cauda equina syndrome, fracture, infection, malignancy or another serious cause.

items.title: Cauda equina assessment
howToTest: Ask directly about difficulty starting urination, reduced awareness of bladder filling, urinary retention and overflow leakage.
Ask about new bowel dysfunction or reduced awareness of defecation.
Ask about new saddle, perineal or genital sensory change.
Ask about new sexual dysfunction associated with the episode.
Ask about bilateral sciatica, bilateral sensory symptoms and progressive weakness.
Where clinically justified and with consent, assess perineal or saddle sensation and examine for objective lower-limb neurological deficits.
normal: No new bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
No new saddle or perineal sensory disturbance.
No bilateral or progressive neurological deficit.
abnormal: New urinary retention, altered bladder sensation or overflow leakage.
New saddle or genital sensory disturbance.
implications: These findings require immediate assessment for cauda equina syndrome.
urgentFeatures: Any new bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
items.importantLimitation: A normal bladder scan, rectal examination, reflex examination or straight-leg raise must not be used alone to exclude cauda equina syndrome.

items.title: Upper motor-neurone screen
howToTest: Assess gait for stiffness, spasticity or a broad-based pattern.
Look for increased tone, brisk reflexes or sustained ankle clonus.
Where within scope, assess the plantar response using a blunt stimulus along the lateral sole.
normal: Normal tone.
No sustained clonus.
Flexor or absent plantar response.
No spastic gait.
implications: These findings suggest spinal cord or central neurological pathology rather than uncomplicated lumbar radiculopathy.

items.title: Alternative-source examination
howToTest: Assess hip movement, particularly internal rotation, and determine whether hip movement reproduces the pain.
Assess the abdomen when pain is atypical, constant, associated with collapse or not reproducible by spinal movement.
Assess pulses, limb temperature, colour and capillary refill when vascular pathology is possible.
Assess renal angles and urinary features when a renal or urinary cause is possible.
normal: No concerning abdominal, vascular, renal or hip findings.
abnormal: Reduced or unequal pulses, or a cold pale limb.
implications: Back pain may be referred from the hip, abdomen, vascular system or urinary tract.
Suspected abdominal or vascular emergency requires immediate escalation rather than spinal imaging.
mustConfirmOrExclude: Hip fracture or acute hip pathology.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm or dissection.
Acute limb ischaemia.
Renal colic, pyelonephritis or urinary obstruction.

sections.title: Common examination patterns
sections.intro: Patterns support clinical reasoning but do not independently confirm or exclude a diagnosis.

items.title: Non-specific mechanical low back pain
commonFindings: Lumbar or paraspinal pain reproduced by movement or position.
Paraspinal tenderness or muscle spasm.
Reduced movement because of pain.
Normal lower-limb power, sensation and reflexes.
Normal gait or an antalgic gait caused by pain.
Straight-leg raise causes back discomfort or hamstring tightness without radicular pain below the knee.
implications: Supports uncomplicated mechanical back pain when the history is reassuring and serious causes have been excluded.

keyTriggers: Image only if serious underlying pathology is suspected or specialist imaging is likely to change management.
guidance: Do not routinely offer imaging for low back pain with or without sciatica in a non-specialist setting.

items.importantLimitation: Movement-related pain and muscular tenderness do not independently exclude fracture, infection, malignancy or referred pathology.

items.title: Lumbar radiculopathy or sciatica
commonFindings: Unilateral shooting, burning or electric leg pain, often extending below the knee.
Straight-leg raise reproduces familiar radicular leg pain.
Dermatomal sensory change.
Myotomal weakness.
Reduced reflex corresponding to the affected root.
implications: Supports nerve-root irritation when the history and examination findings form a consistent pattern.

preferredImaging: MRI in specialist care when the result is likely to change management.
keyTriggers: Suspicion of malignancy, infection or trauma.
guidance: Do not routinely offer imaging for uncomplicated low back pain with sciatica in a non-specialist setting.

items.importantLimitation: Pain distribution is variable and should not be interpreted from a dermatome diagram alone.

items.title: Suspected cauda equina syndrome
commonFindings: New urinary retention, altered bladder sensation or overflow leakage.
New bowel dysfunction.
New saddle or genital sensory disturbance.
New sexual dysfunction.
Bilateral sciatica or progressive lower-limb weakness.
implications: Requires immediate referral for assessment of cauda equina syndrome.

preferredImaging: Urgent MRI through the emergency cauda equina pathway.
keyTriggers: New bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
guidance: Refer immediately for assessment when severe low back pain radiating into the leg is accompanied by new bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction, or new perineal numbness.

items.importantLimitation: No single normal examination finding safely excludes cauda equina syndrome.

items.title: Upper motor-neurone or spinal cord pattern
commonFindings: Bilateral symptoms.
Spastic or broad-based gait.
Increased tone.
Brisk reflexes.
Sustained clonus.
Extensor plantar response.
Sensory disturbance not confined to one lumbar nerve root.
implications: Suggests spinal cord or central neurological pathology rather than uncomplicated mechanical back pain.

preferredImaging: Urgent spinal MRI directed by the clinical level.
CT followed by MRI when acute traumatic spinal injury is suspected with neurological abnormality.
guidance: When traumatic spinal injury is suspected and a neurological abnormality could be attributable to spinal cord injury, perform MRI after CT regardless of whether CT shows the cause.

items.title: Suspected vertebral fracture
commonFindings: Acute pain after trauma, sudden load or minor injury in a patient with fragility-fracture risk.
Focal midline bony tenderness.
Marked pain with movement, standing or weight-bearing.
Possible deformity or new kyphosis.
Neurology may be normal.
implications: May indicate traumatic or osteoporotic vertebral fracture.

preferredImaging: Follow the acute spinal-injury imaging pathway.
CT when thoracic or lumbosacral injury is associated with abnormal neurological signs or symptoms.
MRI after CT when neurological abnormality may be due to spinal cord injury.
keyTriggers: Fragility-fracture risk with acute focal pain.
guidance: Use the NICE spinal-injury pathway for suspected acute traumatic injury.

items.importantLimitation: The absence of bruising, deformity or neurological deficit does not exclude vertebral fracture.

items.title: Suspected spinal metastases or metastatic spinal cord compression
commonFindings: Known cancer with new or progressive back pain.
Constant or progressive pain, night pain or pain disturbing sleep.
Focal spinal tenderness.
Weakness, gait disturbance, sensory loss or bladder or bowel dysfunction when cord or cauda equina compression is present.
implications: Possible spinal metastases, pathological fracture or metastatic spinal cord compression.

keyTriggers: Neurological symptoms or signs suggesting metastatic spinal cord compression.
Known cancer with features suggesting spinal metastases.
guidance: Ensure access to urgent MRI within 24 hours for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression.
Suspected spinal metastases without cord-compression features generally require MRI within 1 week.

items.importantLimitation: A normal neurological examination does not exclude early spinal metastases.

items.title: Suspected spinal infection
commonFindings: Constant or progressive pain.
Focal spinal tenderness.
Fever or systemic illness may be present but can be absent.
Relevant infection risk factors or recent spinal procedure.
implications: Possible discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis or spinal epidural abscess.

preferredImaging: Urgent spinal MRI through the hospital pathway.
keyTriggers: Systemic illness, infection risk or neurological deficit.
guidance: Suspected infection is outside the routine non-specific low-back-pain pathway.

items.importantLimitation: A normal temperature or early normal plain X-ray does not exclude spinal infection.

items.title: Hip pathology presenting as back or buttock pain
commonFindings: Groin, buttock or anterior-thigh pain.
Reduced or painful hip internal rotation.
Pain reproduced more by hip than lumbar movement.
Difficulty weight-bearing with a normal lumbar neurological examination.
implications: Consider hip osteoarthritis, occult fracture or acute joint pathology.

preferredImaging: Urgent hip X-ray when fracture is suspected; further imaging if suspicion persists despite normal X-ray.
keyTriggers: Trauma, inability to weight-bear, shortening or external rotation.

items.title: Renal or urinary source
commonFindings: Flank or loin pain rather than central lumbar pain.
Renal-angle tenderness.
Haematuria, urinary symptoms, fever or vomiting.
Normal lower-limb neurological examination.
implications: Consider renal colic, pyelonephritis or urinary obstruction.

preferredImaging: Follow the renal or urinary imaging pathway rather than spinal imaging.
keyTriggers: Fever or rigors, anuria, solitary kidney, renal impairment or uncontrolled symptoms.

items.title: Abdominal or vascular source
commonFindings: Back pain with abdominal pain, collapse, hypotension, pallor or diaphoresis.
Abdominal tenderness or pulsatile mass.
Reduced or unequal pulses, or a cold pale limb.
Pain not reliably reproduced by spinal movement.
implications: Consider abdominal aortic aneurysm, dissection, acute limb ischaemia or other abdominal pathology.

preferredImaging: Emergency vascular or abdominal imaging through the receiving-hospital pathway.
keyTriggers: Collapse, haemodynamic compromise, pulsatile mass or limb ischaemia.

sections.title: Focused safety-netting
sections.intro: Use the standard emergency statement, then add the diagnosis-specific warning features.

items.title: Back pain
safetyNetting: Call 999 for any significant deterioration, including difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse, reduced consciousness or any immediate concern.

Seek urgent reassessment for new difficulty passing urine, urinary retention or incontinence; loss of bowel control; saddle or genital numbness; new or worsening leg weakness; bilateral leg symptoms; inability to walk; fever or rigors; or rapidly worsening or uncontrolled pain.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting does not make discharge appropriate when serious pathology has not been adequately excluded.
